Today I built the whole space station with the building blocks Tarun gave me for my birthday. I started after breakfast and I thought it was maybe ten o'clock, but then Mummy called me for lunch and it was two! I didn't even hear her the first time. The hardest bit was the round window. Nilesh

Neelam, you're asking why I'm smiling at your brother, lying on the floor with his blocks. Let me, your Bidisha Didima, tell you.
When I was nine, in Shillong, my father brought home a metal building set from a fair: little nuts and bolts and strips with holes. My brothers lost interest in a day. I didn't.
I built a bridge first. Then a windmill that actually turned. I remember sitting on the verandah floor, the light moving across it, and my mother calling me for lunch, then for tea. I didn't hear either time.
Some bolts wouldn't fit. I'd get so cross. Then I'd try another way, and it would click, and I'd feel a happiness that went all the way through me.
That was the first time I learned how to pay attention to one thing for hours. I became an engineer, you know.

Last summer at Nani's house, my cousin Nitin and I tried to make a marble run out of an old building set. I'm Arohi, and I was ten then.
The first slope was too steep and the marble flew off. The second was too flat and it stopped. I kept changing the angle one little bit at a time.
Nani put a plate of mango slices beside me. I didn't see it. Nitin got bored and went out to play cricket. I didn't hear him leave. The ceiling fan clicked, the neighbour's radio played, and I only heard the marble.
When it finally rolled all the way from the top to the bottom, I jumped and shouted. The mango slices were warm by then, and Nani laughed at me.
I still remember that feeling, like the whole world was just the marble.
